title: Socio‐demographic drivers of hunting, trade and local ecological knowledge of the yellow‐casqued hornbill (Ceratogymna elata) in the Ebo forest, Cameroon
content:
Using interviews with 267 respondents across 21 villages surrounding Cameroon's Ebo forest, we found that knowledge, hunting and trade of the Vulnerable yellow-casqued hornbill were structured mainly by age, residency, gender and occupation rather than by geographic proximity alone. Conservation should therefore combine community monitoring led by knowledgeable permanent residents with targeted enforcement along urban-rural trade routes and measures that reduce dependence on the species.


Abstract

The yellow-casqued hornbill (Ceratogymna elata) a Vulnerable African forest species, faces mounting pressure from hunting and trade, yet conservation interventions frequently fail because the social contexts that shape its exploitation remain poorly understood. We examined the drivers of hunting, trade, and local ecological knowledge (LEK) of the species in communities surrounding the Ebo forest, Cameroon, using semi-structured questionnaires (n = 267) and multivariate analyses, including principal coordinates of neighbour matrices (PCNM). Hornbill use was driven by overlapping cultural, taste-related, and livelihood factors, whereas trade and knowledge retention were structured primarily by socio-demographic characteristics such as age, residency status, and gender, rather than how close communities were to each other. Detailed ecological knowledge was concentrated among older, permanent residents, whereas hunting and trade were embedded within broader, generalist wild meat consumption and trade systems rather than reflecting nutritional dependence on the species. These findings indicate that uniform hunting bans are poorly aligned with the social mechanisms that govern use of the species. Practical implication. Effective conservation should move beyond generic bans towards socially differentiated strategies. In particular, managers should (a) formalize partnerships with knowledgeable permanent residents to support community-based monitoring, and (b) target enforcement at urban and rural trade nodes to disrupt commercial flows while supporting rural protein and livelihood alternatives.
